issues.body: `ends_operand` excludes `>` because that byte may be the greater-than operator, but `>` also terminates an IRI operand. Consequently, after scanning the first IRI in `FILTER(<http://ex/a><1&&FLTR(?o)&&?b>2)`, `prev` is `>` and the following compact `<` is treated as an IRIREF opener. Its body is IRIREF-legal through the later `>`, so the scanner skips `FLTR` and fails to suggest `FILTER`. An IRI is a valid primary expression, and SPARQL punctuation does not require whitespace, so this is another real acceptance-set mismatch in the same class as round 2. The added tests cover variable, numeric/call-ending operands and IRIs used as terms, but not an IRI operand immediately preceding less-than.
issues.fix_hint: Track the preceding token's lexical kind (for example, IRI operand versus `>` operator) instead of only its final byte, or use the SPARQL lexer/parser context to classify `<`. Add a real-path regression for `FILTER(<http://ex/a><1&&FLTR(?o)&&?b>2)` asserting that `FLTR` survives and suggests `FILTER`, while retaining coverage for a greater-than operator followed by a genuine IRI.
issues.title: Compact less-than after an IRI operand still swallows diagnostics

verdict.summary: The compact variable-comparison regression is now covered, but the underlying lexical ambiguity remains unresolved. `opens_iriref` reduces the preceding token to its final byte and deliberately excludes `>` from operand endings. That makes a genuine IRI operand followed immediately by `<` look like an IRIREF opener; if a later `>` occurs, `iriref_end` swallows the intervening misspelled keyword. The round-2 correctness class therefore remains at major severity.
